---
title: "Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms"
subtitle: "Two safeties who are deep defenders and run stoppers at the same time, the corner rules that make it work, the half-and-half and trap versions, and why the NFL turned to it after 2018."
description: "Quarters (Cover 4) as a pattern-match coverage: the read safety and his three answers to the inside receiver, the MOD and MEG cornerback rules, how quarters safeties fit the run from depth, Cover 6 (quarter-quarter-half) against trips, Palms (2-read, trap coverage) and the corner who jumps the out, how the defense picks a call and survives motion, why two-high match coverage spread through the NFL from 2018 to 2025 (with the charting data and its source break), and where it breaks: light-box runs, the bootleg flood and the running back's wheel."
glossary:
  Quarters: {def: "A two-deep zone coverage in which the two cornerbacks and the two safeties each start with a deep quarter of the field but play it with match rules: each corner takes the outside receiver (#1) if he goes deep, each safety reads the inside receiver (#2) and also helps against the run. Only three defenders are left underneath.", aliases: ["Cover 4"]}
  "Cover 6": "A split-field coverage that plays quarters on one half of the field and Cover 2 on the other (quarter-quarter-half): usually quarters toward the formation's strength or the wide side, and a squat corner with a deep-half safety on the other side."
  Palms: {def: "A two-high coverage played on one side of the field in which the cornerback and safety trade jobs when the inside receiver (#2) breaks out quickly: the corner jumps (traps) #2's short out or flat route and the safety takes the outside receiver (#1) deep. If #2 goes vertical, the safety carries him and the corner plays #1 man to man.", aliases: ["2-read", "Trap coverage"]}
  MOD: {def: "Man only deep: a cornerback rule in match coverage. The corner covers the outside receiver man-to-man if he runs a deep route (anything past about 5 yards), but if the receiver breaks his route off short (about 5 yards or less) the corner passes him to the underneath defenders and drops into his deep zone.", aliases: ["Man only deep"]}
  MEG: {def: "Man everywhere he goes: a cornerback rule in match coverage. The corner covers his receiver man-to-man on every route, short or deep, which frees the defenders who would otherwise help him for other jobs.", aliases: ["Man everywhere he goes"]}
  "Read safety": "A safety whose job is decided after the snap by one key receiver, usually the inside receiver on his side (#2): he covers #2 if #2 goes deep, helps on the outside receiver if #2 goes short or out, and comes down to fit the run if #2 blocks. The quarters safety is the classic read safety."

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import os
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import RegularPolygon, FancyArrowPatch, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, offense, defense, routes as r, show_animation, style, draw_marker
from gridiron.play import MARKER_R

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
FIELD_W = 160 / 3


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- alignments used all chapter
def pro_2x2():
    """11 personnel, shotgun 2x2 with the tight end attached: X (on the line) and H (slot, off the
    ball) to the left; Y in-line on the right and Z wide right, off the ball. Seven on the line:
    five linemen, X and Y. On the right #1 is Z and #2 is Y; on the left #1 is X and #2 is H."""
    out = []
    for p in offense("gun_2x2"):
        if p.key == "Y":
            p = p.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8)
        elif p.key == "Z":
            p = p.moved(d=-1.5, w=15.0)
        out.append(p)
    return out


def spread_2x2():
    """11 personnel 2x2 with the tight end detached as the right slot (gridiron's gun_2x2)."""
    return offense("gun_2x2")


QUARTERS = {"LCB": (7.5, -15.6), "RCB": (7.5, 15.6), "FS": (9.5, -6.5), "SS": (9.5, 6.5),
            "NB": (4.8, -6.2), "MIKE": (4.8, 1.6), "WILL": (4.8, -2.4)}


def quarters_vs(off, moves=None, sde_9=True):
    """Nickel (4-2-5) quarters shell: corners 7-8 yards off with a slight outside shade; safeties
    9-10 yards deep, a few yards inside a slot or over/just outside an attached tight end
    (shallower and narrower than Cover 2 safeties); the nickel ($) at an apex over the left slot;
    the Mike and Will in the box. sde_9 puts the strong-side end outside an attached tight end
    (a 9 technique) so he can set the edge."""
    m = dict(QUARTERS)
    m.update(moves or {})
    out = []
    for p in defense("nickel", "two_high", off):
        if p.key in m:
            p = p.moved(d=m[p.key][0], w=m[p.key][1])
        if p.key == "SDE" and sde_9:
            p = p.moved(w=5.9)
        if p.pos == "CB":
            p = p.moved(label="CB")
        out.append(p)
    return out


def protect(p, rushers=("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE")):
    """Five linemen set, four rushers engage them: enough to show it is a pass, no more."""
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where wide receivers and safeties stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def ruler(fld, play, widths=False, fs=6.5):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) down the left edge of the field window;
    widths=True also marks the hash marks and the painted numbers along the bottom edge.
    Drawn on the Field's axes: gridiron has no ruler."""
    ax = fld.ax
    x_left = FIELD_W - fld.y1 + 0.35
    for d in range(5, 41, 5):
        y = play.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            ax.text(x_left, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == 5 else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                    ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    if widths:
        y = fld.x0 + 0.9
        for yb, txt in ((23.58, "hash"), (FIELD_W - 23.58, "hash"), (13.0, "numbers"), (FIELD_W - 13.0, "numbers")):
            if fld.y0 + 2.5 <= yb <= fld.y1 - 2.5:
                ax.text(FIELD_W - yb, y, txt, fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center",
                        zorder=12, style="italic",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def say(fld, play, text, at, fs=7.0, color=None, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A small boxed on-field label at (d, w), sized independently of Play.note."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fs, color=color or style.INK, ha=ha, va="center",
                zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5))


def clip(fld):
    """Crop the axes to the drawn field window, so players outside a zoomed window don't
    stretch the picture past the turf. (gridiron draws every player; this trims the view.)"""
    fld.ax.set_xlim(FIELD_W - fld.y1, FIELD_W - fld.y0)
    fld.ax.set_ylim(fld.x0, fld.x1)
    for a in list(fld.ax.texts) + list(fld.ax.patches) + list(fld.ax.lines):
        a.set_clip_on(True)
    return fld


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- frame strips (print version of an animation)
def ghost_marker(ax, x, y, label, ppy, color=style.DEFENSE):
    """A hollow, dashed defender: where he stood at the snap."""
    ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARKER_R * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                facecolor="none", edgecolor=color, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6))
    if label:
        ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", color=color, fontweight="bold", zorder=6,
                fontsize=max(4.0, min(8.5, ppy * 0.75)))


def snapshot(play, t, ax=None, ghosts=(), lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 19.5), notes=(), show_ruler=False):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, with faint trails since the snap and dashed outlines
    (`ghosts`) where the chosen defenders stood at the snap."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    for n in notes:
        q.note(*n)
    fld = clip(q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False))
    ax, ppy = fld.ax, fld.pts_per_yard()
    no_numbers(ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, play, fs=5.5)
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.side == "off" and pl.pos not in ("WR", "TE", "RB"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(0, t, 30)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
            continue
        xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
        if pl.side == "off":
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.45, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
    if t > 0.05:
        for k in ghosts:
            x0, y0 = P(*play.position(k, 0.0))
            ghost_marker(ax, float(x0), float(y0), play.players[k].label, ppy)
    bx, by = P(*play.ball_position(t))
    bd = np.array(play.ball_position(t))
    in_flight = any(k == "pass" and t > tr and np.hypot(*(bd - np.array(play.position(to, t)))) > 1.2
                    for k, to, tr in play.ball_events)
    if not in_flight:                             # tuck a held ball beside its holder so his letter stays readable
        bx, by = float(bx) + 1.0, float(by) + 0.35
    for kind, _, t_rel in play.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass" and t > t_rel:          # a thrown ball: draw its flight so far
            sx, sy = P(*play.ball_position(t_rel))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(bx), float(by)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9))
    draw_marker(ax, float(bx), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, ghosts=(), lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 19.5), notes_at=None,
          width_in=6.5, ncols=2):
    """Panels at chosen moments of one play, ghosts kept on every post-snap panel."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.32)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        snapshot(play, t, ax=ax, ghosts=ghosts, lateral=lateral, window=window,
                 notes=(notes_at or {}).get(i, ()), show_ruler=(i == 0))
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6, w_pad=0.4)
    h = [Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)),
               label="Dashed outline: where he stood at the snap"),
         Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="Defender's path"),
         Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.6, label="Offensive player's path")]
    fig.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=3, fontsize=7.2, frameon=False)
    return fig
```

Second-and-8 near midfield. The offense comes out with three wide receivers and a tight end, two
receivers on each side. Before the snap the broadcast's high camera shows both safeties standing
only about 9 or 10 yards deep, one over each slot receiver, and both cornerbacks backed off 7 or 8
yards. It looks soft. The offense hands the ball off on an inside run, and the first defender to
hit the running back, four yards downfield, is one of those safeties, arriving at full speed from
a spot that looked like pass coverage. Two plays later the offense fakes the same run and throws
deep, and the same safety is running stride for stride with the tight end up the seam. How can one
player be a deep pass defender and a run stopper on the same snap? And why did NFL defenses, which
spent the 2010s crowding an eighth man into the box, spend the next six years taking him back out?
The answer is a coverage with a misleading name: **quarters**.

**You'll be able to…**

- Diagram quarters (Cover 4) against a 2x2 formation and say each defender's rule, not just his
  zone: corners, safeties, the apex defenders and the linebackers.
- Explain how a quarters safety reads the inside receiver (#2) and turns into a man defender, a
  helper on the outside receiver, or a run defender, and why that read is the whole coverage.
- Tell the two cornerback rules apart, MOD and MEG, and say what each one buys and costs.
- Recognise Cover 6 (quarters on one half, Cover 2 on the other) and Palms (the trap) before and
  after the snap.
- Explain, with the data and its caveats, why two-high match coverage spread through the NFL
  between 2018 and 2025, and name the plays that attack it: light-box runs, the bootleg flood and
  the running back's wheel route.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
This is a level 4 chapter. One line each on what it builds on:

- **Shells and the box** ([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)):
  a [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) shell has two safeties deep, one on each
  side of the middle; [one-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-high) has one in the deep
  middle. The [box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box) is the area near the ball where the run is
  defended; a [light box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box) has no more defenders in it
  than the offense has blockers. A defender at an [apex](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-apex)
  stands halfway between the last man in the box and a slot receiver, so he can play either.
- **Formations** ([Spread Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)):
  [2x2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2x2) is two receivers on each side;
  [3x1](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x1) (trips) is three to one side. Receivers are numbered
  from the sideline in on each side: #1 is the widest, then #2, then #3.
- **Zones and matching** ([Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)): the deep field
  splits into thirds, halves or [deep quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-quarter) (about
  13 yards wide each). The [flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flat-zone) is the short area near the
  sideline, the [curl](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-zone) the area between the numbers and
  the hash, the [hook](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hook-zone) the area inside it.
  [Pattern matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pattern-matching) is zone coverage whose
  defenders pick up receivers man-to-man by rule once the routes declare. A
  [press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press) corner lines up within a yard of his receiver; an
  [off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-coverage) corner, 5 to 10 yards away.
- **Cover 2** ([Cover 2 and Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)): two safeties each guard a deep
  half and the [hard corner](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hard-corner) squats in the flat.
- **Run fits** ([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)):
  the [force](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-force-defender) defender turns a run back inside;
  the [alley player](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-alley-player) fills the lane between the force
  and the box; the [plus-one](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-plus-one) is the one more run defender
  than the offense has blockers. Defenders read blockers' "hats": a blocker firing out low means
  run, one popping up tall to protect means pass.
- **Routes and play-action** ([Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd),
  [Play-Action, Boots and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)): a
  [seam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-seam) runs straight upfield between the hash and the
  numbers; an [out](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-out) breaks flat toward the sideline; a
  [slant](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant) breaks sharply inside after a step or two; a
  [dig](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dig) breaks flat inside at 10 to 15 yards; a
  [wheel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wheel) starts toward the flat and turns up the sideline.
  [Four verticals](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-verticals) sends four receivers deep; a
  [flood](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood) puts three receivers at three depths on one side.
  [Play-action](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action) fakes a run before a pass; on a
  [bootleg](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bootleg) the quarterback fakes one way and rolls out the
  other.
- **Who's who:** on offense X is the receiver on the line, Z the receiver off it, Y the tight end,
  U a second tight end and H the third receiver, usually in the slot. In a nickel defense the Mike
  and Will are the two linebackers and the nickel back is the fifth defensive back; a base 4-3
  adds a third linebacker, the [Sam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sam-linebacker).

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (Q quarterback, R running back, C center). Defense
is outlined squares: E and T defensive ends and tackles, M the Mike, W the Will, S the Sam, $ the
nickel back, CB a cornerback, FS and SS the free and strong safety. A **green ring** marks the
players to watch. The faint lines across the field are 5 yards apart from the line of scrimmage
(the blue line), and the small numbers on the left edge give the depth; the short ticks are the
hash marks. Solid arrows are offensive routes, dashed orange arrows defenders' movements, the
dotted brown arrow a pass. In the Predict-the-play figures the orange line is the
[line to gain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-line-to-gain), where the first down is.
:::

## Quarters in one picture: four deep, but not really

Start with the name, because it misleads almost everyone.
**[Quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarters)**, also called
**[Cover 4](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-4)**, is a two-high coverage in which four
defenders, the two cornerbacks and the two safeties, each start with a deep quarter of the field,
a lane about 13 yards wide (hence the "4" in [the numbering system](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)).
If that were the whole story, quarters would be a passive coverage: four defenders guarding deep
grass, three underneath, plenty thrown in front of them. But each of those four deep defenders has
a *rule* that tells him whom to cover once the receivers start running, and two of those rules
point the safeties forward, not back. Here are the alignment and the rules against the NFL's most
common formation, a 2x2 set with the tight end attached.

::: {#cell-fig-c4-match .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = pro_2x2()
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off), los=35, to_go=None)
for w in (-19.0, -6.5, 6.5, 19.0):
    p.zone((18.0, w), (7.0, 12.2), "deep ¼")
for key, txt in (("X", "#1"), ("H", "#2"), ("Y", "#2"), ("Z", "#1")):
    p.note(txt, at=(p.players[key].d - 3.2, p.players[key].w))
p.highlight("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 22.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p, widths=True)
say(fld, p, "CB: MOD on #1\n(man if he goes deep)", (12.0, -18.3), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "CB: MOD on #1", (11.5, 20.5), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "FS: read #2", (12.6, -7.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "SS: read #2", (12.6, 7.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "$: wall #2,\nthen the flat", (2.6, -11.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "W: run, then hook", (7.0, -4.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "M: run, then Y's flat", (7.0, 5.4), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "E: edge,\njams Y", (-2.5, 9.6), fs=6.3)
plt.show()
```

:::


Go around the picture one position at a time.

- **The corners** line up 7 or 8 yards off the outside receiver (#1), square or with a slight
  outside shade, eyes on him. Their rule, MOD, gets its own section below. The short version: if
  #1 runs deep, the corner has him man-to-man; if #1 runs a short route, the corner lets him go and
  drops into his deep quarter.
- **The safeties** are the heart of the coverage. They line up 8 to 10 yards deep (some teams 10 to
  12): a few yards inside a slot receiver, or over or just outside an attached tight end, who is
  already inside the box. That's much shallower and narrower than a
  [Cover 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd) safety, who has to reach the sideline and so stands at
  12 to 14 yards, outside the hash. The quarters safety doesn't have a sideline to reach. His real
  job is to read the inside receiver.
- **The apex defender**, here the nickel back on the slot side, stands between the tackle and the
  slot, 4 or 5 yards deep. Against a pass his first job is to *wall* #2: get in the slot receiver's
  path from the inside and keep him from running freely up the seam, so the safety behind has time
  to read him. Then he takes the first receiver who comes to the flat, the running back included.
- **The linebackers** read run first. Against a pass they drop to the hook zones and take the
  running back if he runs up the middle. On the tight end's side there is no apex defender, so the
  strong-side linebacker (here the Mike) is the first man to the flat if the tight end releases
  outside.
- **The front** rushes four. The end outside the tight end is the edge (contain) player against
  runs to his side, and he can jam the tight end on his way out.

Now count the defenders against the two receivers on one side. On the slot side: the corner, the
safety, the apex defender and, a step inside, a linebacker. On the tight end's side: the corner,
the safety, the Mike and the end. Four players against two receivers, with the back as a possible
third. Coaches like to say quarters is really "four over two" on each side, not four deep, and
that everyone deep is also, depending on what the receivers do, a man defender or a run defender.
That is what makes quarters a [pattern-matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pattern-matching)
coverage, and the purest one in common use.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game's play menu, "Cover 4" usually draws four blue deep zones and three short ones,
and the defenders drop to them like spot-drop zone players. If the real coverage worked that way
it would be a [prevent defense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-prevent-defense) (the soft,
everyone-deep look teams use to protect a late lead, covered in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)): four
defenders guarding grass 15 yards deep while the offense completes everything underneath. Real
quarters is a *read* coverage. The deep quarters are starting points; the receivers' first steps
decide who covers whom, and the two safeties spend the first second of every snap deciding whether
they are deep defenders at all. If you remember one thing from this chapter, make it this:
**quarters safeties play the inside receiver, not a zone.**
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**What it solves.** A defense wants two things that normally conflict: two safeties deep, so the
offense can't hit an explosive pass over the top, and an extra run defender, so it can't run the
ball down its throat. Quarters gets both from the same two players. Standing at 9 or 10 yards
instead of 13, a safety is close enough to the line to fit a run in time and deep enough to carry
a receiver up the seam.

**What it gives up.** The shallow, inside-leaning safeties are reading, and anything that makes
them read wrong hurts: a run fake, a receiver whose release looks like a block, a route that
starts one way and ends another. With only three defenders underneath, the short outside throws
(the quick out, the hitch, the flat) belong to the offense unless a corner or an apex defender
takes them away. Quarters trades a few easy short completions for no deep ones, and asks its
safeties to be right.
:::

## The read safety: one key, three answers

The quarters safety is the clearest example of a
**[read safety](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-read-safety)**: a safety whose job is decided
after the snap by a single key receiver, usually #2 on his side. Coaches teach it as three
answers to one question, *what did #2 do?*

::: {#cell-fig-read-safety .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def read_panel(ax, branch):
    off = pro_2x2()
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("SS")
    if branch == "vert":
        p.route("Y", r.seam(18)); p.route("Z", r.go(18))
        p.drop("SS", (19.0, 5.2), speed=5.0); p.drop("RCB", (19.5, 16.3), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.5))
        title, txt, at = "#2 goes vertical: carry him", "SS: man on #2", (11.5, 9.6)
    elif branch == "out":
        p.route("Y", r.flat(2.0, 7.0)); p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 8))
        p.drop("SS", (8.4, 11.0), speed=5.0); p.drop("RCB", (14.5, 15.0), speed=3.5)
        p.drop("MIKE", (3.2, 10.0), speed=4.5)     # first man to the flat on the tight end's side
        title, txt, at = "#2 goes out: help on #1", "SS: bracket #1\ninside", (16.5, 7.0)
    else:
        p.block("Y", "SDE")
        p.block("RT", "MIKE"); p.block("RG", "SDT"); p.block("C", "WDT")
        p.run("RB", [(1.5, 1.6), (5.2, 3.8)], speed=6.0); p.handoff("RB", 0.6)   # aimed at the C gap
        p.drop("SS", (5.6, 5.8), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (9.5, 15.4), speed=1.0)
        title, txt, at = "#2 blocks: run, fill the alley", "SS: alley\nplayer", (15.5, 6.5)
    fld = clip(p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-3.5, 21.5), window=(-6.5, 22.5), title=False))
    no_numbers(ax)
    say(fld, p, "#2", (-3.2, 4.8), fs=6.5)
    say(fld, p, "#1", (-4.0, 15.0), fs=6.5)
    if branch == "out":
        say(fld, p, "M: first man\nto the flat", (5.8, 7.0), fs=6.0)
    say(fld, p, txt, at, fs=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.2, loc="left", color=style.INK)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
for ax, b in zip(axes, ("vert", "out", "run")):
    read_panel(ax, b)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

Middle: Y releases to the flat, so the safety has no #2 to cover; he works to the outside receiver (#1) and sits inside him, taking away Z's in-breaking route (here a dig) while the corner stays over the top: a bracket. The Mike, the first man to the flat on the tight end's side, runs to Y. 1. **#2 goes vertical: carry him.** If the inside receiver runs up the seam, the safety covers
   him, man-to-man, as deep as he goes. With the corner on #1, every vertical route on that side
   has a defender on top of it.
2. **#2 goes short or out: help on #1.** If #2 runs to the flat or breaks off a short route, the
   safety has nobody to cover, so he turns to the outside receiver and sits *inside* him. Now #1
   has the corner outside and over the top and the safety inside: a
   [bracket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bracket), two defenders on one receiver. The dig and
   the post, the routes that hurt quarters corners most because they break away from the corner's
   outside position, run straight into the safety. (If #2 runs inside, across the field, many
   systems tell the safety to pass him to the linebackers and look for work: #1 breaking in, or a
   crossing route coming from the other side.)
3. **#2 blocks: it's a run, so fill.** If #2 is a tight end who blocks, or a slot receiver who
   steps up to block the apex defender, and the linemen in front of the safety fire out low, the
   safety reads run and comes downhill. In the language of
   [Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd),
   he becomes the alley player: he fills the lane between the edge and the box, inside-out, and he
   is the defense's plus-one.

What counts as "vertical"? Most staffs draw the line where the corner's rule does, at about 5
yards. A #2 who breaks out or in before that is short; a #2 still pushing upfield past it is
vertical, and the safety stays on top of him until he breaks. If he then curls or digs at 10 or
12 yards, the safety sits over it with a hook defender underneath. Exact depths vary by staff.

Why does one receiver make such a good key? Because #2's release tells the safety, almost
instantly, both run-or-pass and where the danger is. A receiver who blocks is the strongest run
signal there is; one who releases vertical *is* the danger; one who runs to the flat isn't a deep
threat, so the deep threat must be the outside man.
Good safeties check it against the linemen in front of them: low hats confirm the run, but a #2
who "blocks" while the linemen pop up tall to pass-protect is selling a fake, a
[chip](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-chip) before a release or a play-action block. That check
takes a beat, and it is the read's weak spot, as the bootleg section will show.

That also explains where the safety stands. He has to be shallow enough to fill the alley before
the running back gets through it, and deep enough to turn and run with a tight end up the seam
without being beaten over the top. Nine or ten yards is the compromise. TCU's Gary Patterson, one
of the coaches who made quarters famous in college football, taught his safeties not to backpedal
at the snap at all but to shuffle flat-footed and read, because a safety rocking backward can't
come forward in time.[^patterson] Watch one quarters safety for a whole game on the All-22 film
(the high, wide camera coaches use) and you'll be surprised how rarely he ends the play deep.

### Four verticals: the stress test quarters was built for

The best way to see why match rules matter is the play that broke spot-drop zones in the 1980s
and 1990s: [four verticals](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-verticals), four receivers
running straight up the field. Against spot-drop Cover 3, four vertical routes meet three deep
defenders, and one of them has to guard two receivers ([Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) shows
the seam opening). Against quarters, the rules simply add up.

::: {#cell-fig-four-verts-c4 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = spread_2x2()
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"NB": (4.8, 6.2), "WILL": (4.8, -6.2), "MIKE": (4.8, 0.0)}), los=35, to_go=None)
p.route("X", r.go(22)); p.route("Z", r.go(22)); p.route("H", r.seam(21)); p.route("Y", r.seam(21))
p.dropback(2.5)
protect(p)
p.drop("LCB", (22.5, -14.6), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (22.5, 14.6), speed=5.5)
p.drop("FS", (21.0, -8.0), speed=5.5); p.drop("SS", (21.0, 8.0), speed=5.5)
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -9.0)); p.drop("NB", (8.0, 9.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 0.0))
p.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 25.0))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, "corners: #1 deep", (13.5, -21.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "safeties: #2 deep", (13.0, 0.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "$, W: wall,\nthen sink", (14.0, 12.0), fs=6.4)
plt.show()
```

Notice what the defense didn't need: a decision. Nobody had to choose between two receivers; the
rules assigned one defender to each. That doesn't make four verticals hopeless. Every deep defender is now man-to-man with
nobody in the deep middle, so a great outside receiver against a corner (a fade, a back-shoulder
throw) can still win, and the running back checking down against three underneath defenders is
the offense's release valve. Offenses also built concepts aimed straight at the safety's read:
[dagger](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dagger) (a deep dig behind a clearing seam) and
[scissors](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scissors) (a post by #1 crossing a corner route by #2),
both in [Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd), and the weaknesses
section below adds three more.

## The corner's rule: MOD and MEG

The safety's rule only works if the corner's rule fits with it. Quarters teams use two, and the
names come from the playbook vocabulary that spread out of Nick Saban's defenses (more on that
history below).

**[MOD](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mod)**, short for
**[man only deep](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-only-deep)**, is the standard quarters
corner rule. The corner covers #1 man-to-man *if #1 runs a deep route*. If #1 breaks his route off
short, about 5 yards or less (a hitch, a quick out, a slant, a shallow cross), the corner doesn't
chase him. He passes him to the underneath defenders and drops into his deep quarter, looking for
the next threat to come into it. "Deep" here means anything past that 5-yard line, so a 12-yard dig
or a curl counts: the corner stays on it. That is nearly word for word the rule Cameron Soran
decoded from Saban's playbooks, which also give the other two clauses of the same call. The
safety: take all of #2 vertical; if #2 isn't vertical, bracket #1. The apex defender: take the
first man to the flat, rerouting #2 first if he starts vertical.[^soran-mod]

**[MEG](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-meg)**, short for
**[man everywhere he goes](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-everywhere-he-goes)**, is the
other rule. The corner covers #1 on every route, short or deep, no exceptions. You met MEG in
[Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) as the backside corner's rule in a trips check; it shows up
wherever a defense needs one corner to take care of his man alone so that the defenders around
him can do something else.

::: {#cell-fig-mod-meg .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def modmeg_panel(ax, kind):
    off = spread_2x2()
    mv = {"NB": (4.8, -6.4)}
    if kind == "MEG":
        mv["LCB"] = (1.0, -14.1)                     # MEG from press, inside shade on X
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, mv), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.route("X", r.slant(2, 6)); p.route("H", r.path((10, 0), (18, 5.5)))
    if kind == "MOD":
        p.highlight("LCB", "FS")
        p.drop("LCB", (15.5, -15.6), speed=4.0)
        p.drop("FS", (16.5, -13.2), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("NB", (5.0, -10.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -4.0))
        title = "MOD: #1 breaks short, so the corner zones off"
        lab = [("slant: left to\nthe underneath\ndefenders", (9.0, -21.0)),
               ("corner route:\nCB and FS\nboth on it", (20.5, -12.5))]
    else:
        p.highlight("LCB", "NB")
        p.drop("LCB", (3.8, -12.3), speed=5.0); p.drop("LCB", (6.6, -10.6), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("FS", (16.5, -14.5), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("NB", (10.0, -12.0), speed=5.0); p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -4.5))
        title = "MEG: the corner goes wherever #1 goes"
        lab = [("CB alone\non the slant", (9.0, -21.0)),
               ("$ freed: sinks\nunder the corner\nroute; FS over it", (20.5, -11.5))]
    fld = clip(p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-25.0, 3.5), window=(-6.5, 24.0), title=False))

The trade is clear in the two panels.

- **MOD keeps the corner deep and gives the defense extra help on the dangerous routes.** Short
  routes by #1 are left to the defenders already in front of them (the apex defender, the
  linebackers), who can rally and tackle for a short gain. The corner, freed from the short route,
  becomes a second defender on whatever goes deep on his side, often #2 breaking outside, as here.
  The cost: the short throw to #1 is there if the underneath defenders are slow to it, and a
  receiver who fakes short and goes deep (a stop-and-go, a slant-and-go) can catch a MOD corner
  who passed him off too early.
- **MEG locks the corner on his man and frees someone else.** In the figure the freed player is
  the nickel; in the trips checks of
  [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) it is
  a whole safety, who leaves his side to help elsewhere. The cost: the corner is on an island with
  no inside help, and every route that breaks away from him, especially a slant or a dig against
  an off corner, is his problem alone. MEG needs a corner the defense trusts.

A defense picks between them by situation and by personnel. A team with one great corner might
play him MEG on the opponent's best receiver and MOD on the other side. Against a lone receiver in
a trips formation, MEG on the backside corner is the standard way to free the backside safety. And
in the red zone MEG becomes more common, because MOD's escape hatch is gone: with the end line 10
or 15 yards away there is no deep quarter to retreat into, so the short routes *are* the dangerous
ones, and a corner who passes them off has nothing left to guard.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: rules that agree with each other"}
The rules fit together like a contract. MOD says "I'll let #1 go if he's short"; the apex and hook
defenders say "we'll take what comes short, outside and inside"; the safety says "if #2 isn't
vertical, I'll bracket #1," covering the one thing MOD gives up deep. Change one clause, from MOD
to MEG for example, and every other clause shifts with it. That is why match defenses talk so much
before the snap.
:::

## Quarters against the run: the safeties fit from depth

Now the part of quarters that made it a run defense. Look back at the alignment: four defensive
linemen and two linebackers in the box, six defenders, against five offensive linemen and a tight
end, six blockers. By the box count of
[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) that is
a light box: every run defender can be blocked and nobody is left over. A defense playing one-high
would usually have walked its strong safety down to make it seven against six.

Quarters gets its seventh (and sometimes eighth) run defender from 9 or 10 yards away: when #2
blocks and the linemen fire out low, the safety comes downhill into the alley. College coaches with
a 4-3 front call it a "nine-man front," seven defenders near the line plus two safeties who arrive
when the play is a run.

::: {#cell-fig-quarters-runfit .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def run_play():
    off = pro_2x2()
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off), los=35, to_go=None)
    # inside zone right: the line steps right; Y base-blocks the end; the center and right tackle climb
    p.block("LT", "WDE"); p.block("LG", "WDT"); p.block("RG", "SDT"); p.block("Y", "SDE")
    p.block("C", "WILL", speed=2.6); p.block("RT", "MIKE", speed=2.6)
    p.run("RB", [(-4.6, 0.2), (-1.0, 2.6), (2.0, 4.6), (4.0, 6.5)], delay=0.25, speed=6.2, absolute=True)
    p.handoff("RB", 0.6)
    p.route("X", [(2.0, 0.0)], speed=3.0); p.route("Z", [(2.5, 0.0)], speed=3.0)   # stalk blocks
    p.route("H", r.seam(18))                                                     # H releases
    for k, to in (("WDE", (1.2, -4.6)), ("WDT", (1.3, -1.6)), ("SDT", (1.3, 2.0)), ("SDE", (1.4, 6.2))):
        p.path(k, [to], absolute=True, speed=1.0)
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.6, 2.6)], absolute=True, speed=2.0); p.path("WILL", [(3.8, 0.4)], absolute=True, speed=2.0)
    p.drop("SS", (5.2, 7.6), speed=4.6, delay=0.45)      # reads Y's low block: run, so fill the alley
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -8.8), speed=5.0, delay=0.2)     # reads H's release: pass, so stay with him
    p.drop("RCB", (5.5, 13.6), speed=2.2, delay=0.4)     # Z blocks him: the corner comes up outside-in
    p.drop("LCB", (9.0, -15.4), speed=2.0); p.drop("NB", (6.0, -8.0), speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("SS", "FS")
    return p


run_c4 = run_play()
RUN_T = [0.0, 0.5, 1.3, 2.1]

Quarters against inside zone, frame by frame (simulated). Snap: six defenders in the box against six blockers, with both safeties (ringed) 9 to 10 yards deep. +0.5 s: the tight end Y (the strong safety's #2) fires out low to block the end, and the line steps right: run. +1.3 s: the strong safety (SS) is already coming downhill into the alley outside the tight end, while the free safety (FS), whose #2 (H) released up the field, stays with him: H took the FS out of the run fit. +2.1 s: the ball carrier (R, with the brown ball beside him) bends the run outside and the SS meets him three or four yards downfield. The dashed outlines show where the safeties stood at the snap. The run went toward Y, so losing the FS cost the defense nothing here; the text explains why the offense would rather run the other way.
:::
:::


Three things in that play are worth slowing down for.

**The trigger is a read, not a call.** The strong safety didn't know before the snap that this
would be a run. He found out from Y's block in the first half-second, and he went. That is the
difference between quarters and the rotation of
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd), where
a safety is *told* before the snap to come down at the snap, read or no read. The called rotation
arrives sooner, and it is wrong whenever the guess is wrong. The read arrives later, and an honest
pass never pulls it forward, because #2 running a route is a pass read. Its weak spot is the
dishonest run look, a play-action fake and a #2 who pretends to block, which is exactly what the
bootleg flood below attacks.

**He meets the back past the line of scrimmage.** From 9 or 10 yards the safety is a beat later
than a linebacker at 4 or 5, so he typically makes the play three to five yards downfield, roughly
the bargain [Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)
describes for the two-high light box: give up a four-yard run, never a forty-yard pass.

**The other safety went with his receiver.** The free safety's #2, H, released up the field, a pass
read, so the free safety stayed with him and was out of the run fit. Here that cost the defense
nothing, because the run went toward Y and the safety who filled was the play-side one. Now flip
it: run the same play to the left, toward H. H releases, the free safety (now the play-side
safety) goes with him, and the only safety left to fill is the strong safety, on the backside,
arriving late through traffic. That is the offense's main weapon against quarters' run defense,
and it costs the offense little, one fewer blocker on the perimeter (the nickel is left unblocked,
so the back has to beat him). Offenses with a good slot receiver run the ball *away* from the tight
end for exactly this reason, and [RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) go one step further
by letting the quarterback read that safety and throw to the receiver if he comes down anyway.

Had H blocked instead, the free safety still wouldn't have raced to the ball. With the run going
away from him he is the [cutback](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cutback) player, filling late
and inside-out in case the back reverses course, and the first defender who has to see a bootleg
or a reverse coming back his way. Outside the safeties, the end sets the edge on the tight end's
side and the corner comes up once Z blocks him; on the slot side the nickel is both the force
player and the first man to the flat, the
[overhang defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-overhang-defender) job (the defender outside
the box, over the slot). Names vary by staff; the geometry, an outside defender who forces and a
safety who fills inside him, doesn't.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: run support from the secondary"}
**What it solves.** Most of the time a defense that wants an extra run defender has to *show*
him: a safety walked down to 7 or 8 yards before the snap, which tells the offense to throw.
Quarters hides the extra defender inside a two-high picture and lets the offense's own blocking
call him into the fit. Every running play is met by six defenders in the box plus one or two who
arrive late from depth, and every pass that looks like a pass is met by two safeties who never
left.

**What it gives up.** Time and certainty. The safety arrives after the back has crossed the line,
so quarters gives up more yards per run than an eight-man box, and he must tackle in space with
nobody behind him. And anything that disguises the read attacks the coverage at its heart.
:::

## Cover 6: quarters on one side, Cover 2 on the other

Quarters works beautifully when each side of the formation has two receivers. Formations don't
always cooperate. Against trips, one side has three receivers and the other a lone receiver, and
on the lone receiver's side there is no #2 at all: a read-#2 safety has nothing to read. The most
common fix is to split the field.
**[Cover 6](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-6)** plays quarters on one half of the field and
Cover 2 on the other, which is why coaches also call it *quarter-quarter-half* (the corner and
safety each take a quarter on one side; one safety takes the whole half on the other). The number
is dialect, not law: in Vic Fangio's system the split-field family is Cover 6 and
[Cover 8](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-8), and his Cover 8 flips the halves, putting the
Cover 2 half toward the passing strength
([Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) has the dialect notes).

[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) shows
Cover 6 in its most common NFL use, against a 2x2 set split by field position (quarters to the wide
side, Cover 2 to the short side). Here it is against a 3x1 trips set, one of the formations that
calls for it, with the split made by formation: quarters to the three receivers, Cover 2 to the
lone receiver.

::: {#cell-fig-cover6-3x1 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = offense("gun_trips")
mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 17.6), "SS": (9.5, 8.6), "NB": (4.6, 7.5), "MIKE": (4.8, 2.4), "WILL": (4.8, -2.2),
      "LCB": (5.5, -16.2), "FS": (12.5, -7.0)}
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, mv), los=35, to_go=None)
p.zone((18.0, -13.0), (8.0, 25.0), "deep ½")
p.zone((18.0, 6.5), (7.0, 12.0), "¼"); p.zone((18.0, 19.0), (7.0, 12.0), "¼")
p.zone((3.8, -20.0), (4.0, 8.0), "flat")
p.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 25.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p, widths=True)
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(-6.5, 0.0)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(24.5, 0.0))
fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (6, 4)), zorder=2)
say(fld, p, "COVER 2 HALF", (23.6, -6.5), fs=7.5, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, "QUARTERS", (23.6, 5.0), fs=7.5, weight="bold")
for txt, key in (("#1", "Z"), ("#2", "H"), ("#3", "Y")):
    q = p.players[key]
    say(fld, p, txt, (q.d - 2.6, q.w), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "CB: squat,\nthe flat", (8.6, -20.6), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "FS: deep half\nover X", (15.2, -7.0), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "W: curl/hook", (7.4, -4.6), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "CB: MOD on #1", (11.0, 20.6), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "SS: read #2", (12.3, 9.4), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "$: wall #2", (2.7, 10.8), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "M: carry #3\nif vertical", (7.6, 3.2), fs=6.4)
plt.show()

Left, toward the lone receiver X, Cover 2: the corner squats 5 yards off with outside leverage to take the flat and short outside throws, the Will takes the curl and hook, and the free safety (FS) stands deeper and wider, 12 to 13 yards deep a few yards outside the hash, to take the whole deep half over X. Why put Cover 2 on the lone receiver? Look at what the two defenders on that side are doing to
X. The squat corner sits in front of him, taking away the quick out, the hitch and the flat; the
half-field safety sits over the top of him, taking away the go route. X is bracketed under and
over by two defenders, which is more help than most single receivers ever see. That matters
because offenses put their best receiver alone on the backside of trips precisely to get him a
one-on-one matchup. Cover 6 says no.

The cost is on the trips side, where four defenders (corner, safety, nickel and Mike) handle three
receivers who can all run deep. Nobody is uncovered: the corner has #1, the safety #2 and the Mike
#3 if he runs up the middle. The problem is the matchup. If #2 and #3 both go vertical, the safety
takes #2 and the Mike is left running down the seam with a tight end or a slot receiver, a race
most linebackers lose. That is the trips problem in its purest form, and two-high defenses carry
other answers to it, such as [poach](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-poach) (the backside safety
leaves the lone receiver to his corner and comes across to help on #3), which
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) covers
in detail. Cover 6 is the simplest answer: give the lone receiver to two defenders, and trust four
on three.

Cover 6 is also how Cover 2 survived: too easy to attack as a whole defense
([Cover 2 and Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)), it still earns its keep as *half* of one,
aimed at the short side or a lone receiver. By NFL Next Gen Stats' count, Cover 6 was 9.2% of
coverages in 2025.[^ngs] After the snap the corners give it away, one squatting and one bailing;
the Watch-for-it box at the end has the full sequence.

## Palms: the corner who traps the out

Quarters has one obvious soft spot: the flat, in the first second after the snap. The apex
defender's rule makes him the owner of the flat, but he starts *inside* #2, walling him off the
seam, 4 or 5 yards from where a quick out breaks. On a throw that comes out in about a second he
can't widen in time. The corner is 8 yards deep playing #1, and the safety is reading #2 from 9.
So a quick throw to #2 breaking toward the sideline lands in front of everyone. Offenses learned to
throw it all day: the slot receiver's quick out, the "now" throw to the flat (a cousin of the
[now screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-now-screen)), the out by the slot in a smash-type
concept.

**[Palms](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-palms)** is the answer. The same coverage goes by
**[2-read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2-read)** and, because of what the corner does,
**[trap coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trap-coverage)**. Different staffs use different
names and slightly different rules, but the core is one adjustment on one side of the field:
**the corner reads #2 instead of #1.**

- If #2 breaks *out* quickly (inside the first 5 yards or so), the corner leaves #1 and jumps
  #2's out or flat route. He was 6 or 7 yards deep, square or a little outside #1, with his eyes
  turned in to #2, so he comes forward and outside-in onto the throw instead of chasing it. That
  is the trap.
- The safety, seeing #2 go out, takes #1 deep: he's now the deep defender over the outside
  receiver whom the corner just left. In Saban's version the safety's rule reads: take #1 vertical
  if #2 is out in the first 5 yards; otherwise, take all of #2 vertical, and if #2 isn't vertical,
  bracket #1.[^soran-palms]
- If #2 goes vertical, the safety carries #2 and the corner plays #1 man to man, in most versions
  without the MOD release, so a short route by #1 runs into a corner who is already shallow and
  squeezing.

::: {#cell-fig-palms-trap .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def palms_play():
    off = spread_2x2()
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"LCB": (6.3, -15.9)}), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.route("H", r.out(5.5, 6)); p.route("X", r.path((3, 0.6), (24, 1.4)))
    p.route("Y", r.seam(16)); p.route("Z", r.hitch(6))
    p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 5), side=1)
    p.dropback(2.5); p.pass_to("H", t=1.05)
    protect(p)
    p.drop("LCB", (6.6, -15.8), speed=1.0)                                    # sits and reads #2
    p.path("LCB", [(4.4, -15.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.6, delay=0.45)      # #2 out: drive on it, outside-in
    p.drop("FS", (19.0, -14.6), speed=6.0, delay=0.25)                        # #2 out: take #1 vertical
    p.drop("NB", (5.6, -8.4), speed=3.0); p.drop("NB", (4.4, -11.6), speed=3.5)   # walls H inside, late to widen
    p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 4.0))
    p.drop("SS", (15.0, 6.5)); p.drop("RCB", (8.5, 15.6), speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("LCB", "FS")
    return p


palms = palms_play()
PALMS_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.0]
h6, x6 = palms.position("H", 0.6), palms.position("X", 0.6)
if PDF:
    strip(palms, PALMS_T, ["Snap · it looks like quarters", "+0.6 s · #2 breaks out; CB reads him",
                           "+1.4 s · CB drives on it; FS takes X", "+2.0 s · thrown into the CB"],
          ghosts=("LCB", "FS"), lateral=(-25, 11.5), window=(-9.0, 23.0),
          notes_at={1: [("#2", (float(h6[0]) - 2.6, float(h6[1]))), ("#1", (float(x6[0]) - 2.8, float(x6[1])))],
                    2: [("$ walled H inside:\ntoo late to widen", (-5.4, -10.0))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(palms, times=PALMS_T)

Palms on the offense's left, frame by frame (simulated). Snap: the picture is quarters, except that the corner (CB, ringed) is a yard or so shallower than usual, square to slightly outside X, with his eyes turned in to H, the #2 receiver. +0.6 s: H breaks to the sideline on a quick out at 4 yards; the corner's eyes are on him, and the free safety (FS, ringed) sees it too. +1.4 s: the corner has left X and is driving forward, outside-in, onto the out; the free safety has turned and is taking X deep. The nickel ($), who walled H from the inside, is still yards away from the flat. +2.0 s: the quarterback, who saw an off corner before the snap and thought the out would be open, has thrown it, and the ball arrives with the corner already in the throwing lane. The dashed outlines show where the corner and safety stood at the snap.
:::
:::


Watch the timing. The out route is a rhythm throw: the quarterback decides before the snap, takes
his drop and lets it go as #2 breaks, about a second after the snap. He threw it because the corner
looked like a quarters corner, off and playing the outside receiver. Why would he fall for it if
there is a tell? Because the tell is a yard of depth and a turn of the head, often disguised until
the snap, and a rhythm throw is decided before the snap: the quarterback isn't re-reading the
corner as he lets it go. A Palms corner's eyes were on #2 from the start, and he started forward
the moment #2 broke. Against a throw that travels 15 or more yards across the field, a defender
coming *downhill* onto the route gets to the catch point first. That's how quick outs become
interceptions returned the other way.

Palms also cleans up two routes that trouble [Cover 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd). Against smash (a hitch by #1, a corner route by #2), #2's corner route starts vertical, so
the safety carries it, and the hitch runs into the corner, who is manned up on #1 and sitting on
it. Against a slot's flat route paired with a curl by #1, the corner jumps the flat and the safety,
who no longer has a vertical #2, drives on the curl from inside.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: taking away the throw quarters gives up"}
**What it solves.** Quarters concedes quick outside throws to #2. Palms puts a defender on them
without adding one: the corner, who would have been 8 yards deep over a #1 who isn't going deep,
trades jobs with the safety, who would have had nothing to do once #2 went to the flat.

**What it gives up.** The trap is a guess about the route, and good offenses bait it. A #2 who
breaks out and then turns up the sideline (an out-and-up, or a wheel) runs right past the jumping
corner, and the safety is busy with #1. A #1 who runs a
[double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move) against a safety coming from inside can
win too. And the corner who reads #2 is, for a moment, not watching #1 at all, so a fast #1 on a
quick slant inside him can be open in the first second. Defenses mix Palms with plain quarters for
exactly this reason: a corner who always traps gets beaten by the play designed for him.
:::

How do you spot it? Before the snap, barely: the Palms corner is often a yard or two shallower than
the other corner, with his shoulders and eyes turned in toward the slot. After the snap it's
unmistakable: the corner comes *forward* toward #2 while the safety on that side runs *outward and
deep* over #1, and the two cross like a pair of scissors. Palms is usually played to one side,
often the short side of the field or a 2x2 side, while the other half plays its own call, which
makes it another piece of the split-field toolbox.

## Who decides: calls, checks and motion

Three coverages that look alike before the snap raise an obvious question: how do eleven defenders
know which one they're in? Usually in two layers. The sideline sends in a call for the family, and
the players on each side *check* within it once they see the formation. The corner and safety on a
2x2 side might play quarters or Palms depending on the receivers' splits; a 3x1 set might turn the
call into Cover 6 or a trips check such as poach. A safety or the Mike makes the strength call, by
shout and hand signal, so both halves agree where the split is.

[Motion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion) tests all of that, because motion changes who is
#2. Receivers are recounted from the sideline after every move. If H motions from the left slot
across to the right, the free safety's side suddenly has one receiver and no #2 to read, and the
right side has three. The defense has a second or two to re-declare: the strength flips, the free
safety becomes a lone-receiver-side player (a Cover 2 half, or a poach player watching #3), and the
apex defender usually slides over with the motion, a
[bump](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bump-defensive-adjustment) that keeps everyone in his
zone. Get the re-declaration wrong and two defenders take the same receiver while the new #2 runs
free. That is a big reason offenses motion so much against split-field defenses
([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd) has
the offense's side, [Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)
the defense's answers).

## Why two-high match took over the NFL, 2018 to 2025

None of this was new in 2018. What changed is how much NFL defenses used it. NFL Next Gen Stats
(the league's tracking-data arm) measures how often defenses play a split-safety (two-high)
coverage after the snap: 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018, 37.8% in 2021, 40.4% in 2024 and 42.0% in
2025, the highest since its tracking began. Quarters was the biggest single piece: Cover 4 alone
was 17.2% of 2025 coverages by Next Gen Stats' count, against a 2018–2024 average of 13.9%, with
Cover 2 at 13.9% and Cover 6 at 9.2%.[^ngs-detail]

You can rebuild the trend yourself from the free nflverse data, which carries a coverage label on
each charted play. The labels come from
[charting](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-game-charting): people watching film of every play and
tagging it, here with the coverage they think the defense played. Coverage is tagged essentially
only on passing plays (dropbacks, plays where the quarterback drops back to pass), because on a run
nobody can tell what the coverage would have become. That human judgment is the caveat.

::: {#cell-fig-two-high-trend .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from gridiron.data import nfl

part = nfl().load_participation(list(range(2018, 2026))).to_pandas()
cv = part[part["defense_coverage_type"].notna()].copy()
gid = cv["nflverse_game_id"].str.split("_", expand=True)          # e.g. 2024_02_SF_MIN
cv["season"], cv["week"] = gid[0].astype(int), gid[1].astype(int)
cv = cv[cv["week"] <= np.where(cv["season"] <= 2020, 17, 18)]    # regular season only
cv = cv[~cv["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["BLOWN", "COMBO", "PREVENT"])]
share = pd.crosstab(cv["season"], cv["defense_coverage_type"], normalize="index") * 100
two = share[["COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"]].sum(axis=1)
NGS = {2018: 32.9, 2021: 37.8, 2024: 40.4, 2025: 42.0}            # published, NFL.com (see notes)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 5.4), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.15, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(two.index, two.values, marker="o", ms=4.5, color=style.SERIES[0], label="nflverse charting labels")
ax.scatter(list(NGS), list(NGS.values()), s=46, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.6,
           zorder=3, label="NFL Next Gen Stats (published)")
for yr, v in two.items():
    ax.text(yr, v + (-2.0 if yr == 2024 else 1.0), f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[0])
ax.set_ylim(28, 47)
ax.set_ylabel("Two-high, % of dropbacks", fontsize=8.5)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("Two-high coverage after the snap, 2018–2025 regular seasons", fontsize=10)
ax = axes[1]
for col, lab, c in (("COVER_2", "Cover 2", style.MUTED), ("COVER_4", "Quarters (Cover 4)", style.SERIES[2]),

           zorder=3, label="NGS 2025 (published)")
for lab, v in ngs25.items():

ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.0, ncol=1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 31)
ax.set_ylabel("% of dropbacks", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlim(2017.6, 2026.4)

The top panel is the trend, and the two sources agree on it: about a third of dropbacks in 2018,
over 40% by 2022 and again in 2025, with a dip in 2024 that only the nflverse labels show.[^trend]
The bottom panel is a lesson in reading charting data. Through 2022 the components climb together;
after the switch from NGS to FTN charting, quarters appears to collapse while Cover 2 soars. Nothing
like that happened on the field. Two groups of charters drew the line between "two safeties
guarding halves" and "two safeties reading #2" in different places, and NGS's own 2025 counts,
shown as rings, disagree with the FTN labels by close to a factor of two in both directions. Both
are honest. Quarters and Cover 2 look alike before the snap and for a beat after it, and the
difference is in rules a charter has to infer. Palms is the extreme case: on one snap it plays like
quarters, on the next like a corner squatting in the flat, so where it lands depends on who is
charting. Use the total, which is robust, and be careful with the split. (The nflverse data has the
same kind of break in its man/zone labels, which is why [Man Coverage](06-02-man-coverage.qmd)
doesn't chart a man-coverage trend across 2022–2025.)

Why the rise? No single cause, but five reasons show up again and again in coaches' and analysts'
explanations, and they reinforce each other.

1. **Explosive passes became the thing to stop.** The plays that decide games are the long
   completions ([Expected Points and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
   shows why a 40-yard pass is worth so much more than a 4-yard run), and by the late 2010s passing
   was more efficient than ever. The 2018 season was the loudest version: Patrick Mahomes threw 50 touchdown passes in his first year as a starter, and
   the Rams beat his Chiefs 54–51 on a Monday night in November.[^2018] Two deep safeties are the
   most direct protection against the explosive pass, and quarters keeps two deep without giving up
   the run.
2. **Match rules answered the spread passing game.** Offenses built on putting two receivers in
   one zone defender's area ran into zones that followed the receivers.
3. **The extra run defender could come from depth.** A defense that played one-high with an eighth
   man in the box was guessing run every snap, and run-pass options punished that guess
   ([RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)). Quarters' read safeties are harder to put in
   conflict before the snap, because their run job is decided by the play itself.
4. **Two-high pictures disguise everything.** From a two-high shell a defense can play quarters,
   Cover 6, Palms, Cover 2 or 2-Man, or rotate into a one-high coverage at the snap. The more of
   those it plays, the less the quarterback learns before the snap
   ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)).
5. **Coaching trees and a college pipeline.** Coaches who learned split-field quarters in college
   (more below) reached NFL staffs, and one tree in particular spread it: that of Vic Fangio, whose
   two-high defenses in Chicago (as coordinator) and Denver (as head coach, 2019–2021) became the
   model. His story is a case study:
   [Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).

There is a sixth condition that isn't a cause so much as a price of admission: **a four-man rush
that can win.** A light box and two deep safeties work only if four rushers can pressure the
quarterback without help, because nobody else is coming. Quarters teams can blitz, usually with an
apex defender or a linebacker, but every extra rusher comes out of the four-over-two, so much of
their pressure is still four rushers chosen in a surprising way, a
[simulated pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd). The defenses that
lived in two-high were also the ones with dominant interior rushers, a pattern you'll see in the
film room.

And offenses answered. If quarters invites the run against a light box, run it; if it reads #2,
make #2 a blocker. The 2024 and 2025 seasons brought more two- and three-tight-end personnel and
more snaps under center, the subject of [The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd).

### A short history: from Cleveland to East Lansing and Iowa City

Four defenders deep is an old idea; prevent defenses have used it for decades. Quarters as a read
coverage whose safeties fit the run is mostly a product of 1990s and 2000s college football, with
one important root in the NFL.

That root is Cleveland. Nick Saban was Bill Belichick's defensive coordinator with the Browns from
1991 to 1994, and the pattern-matching rules the two developed there, first for Cover 3 and then
for the quarters family, went with Saban to Michigan State as head coach in 1995 and later to LSU
and Alabama.[^cleveland] Saban's vocabulary is the one this chapter has been using (MOD, MEG,
Palms), plus "Cover 7" for his quarters-based split-field family
([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)) and
"Rip" and "Liz" in his match Cover 3 ([Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)). One set of match
rules, several coverages: that's the Saban-Belichick inheritance. Like most who-invented-it stories, this one has rivals;
other staffs were building match rules at the same time, and the coverage numbers themselves meant
different things in different buildings.

Michigan State kept the quarters thread alive after Saban left. Under head coach Mark Dantonio, who
had coached Saban's secondary in East Lansing, and defensive coordinator Pat Narduzzi (2007–2014),
the Spartans' 4-3 quarters became one of the most studied defenses in the country (the film room
has its best season). Narduzzi came to Cover 4 the hard way: in 2002, as a Northern Illinois
assistant, he watched Miami (Ohio)'s Ben Roethlisberger throw for 525 yards against his defense's
two-deep look, and when he became Miami's defensive coordinator the next year, by his own telling
at a 2014 clinic, his answer was Cover 4.[^narduzzi]

Iowa is the other long-running reference point. Norm Parker installed his 4-3 defense when Kirk
Ferentz took over the program at the end of the 1990s, and Phil Parker (no relation), the defensive
coordinator since 2012, kept it: a front that holds up against the run while the safeties play
split-field quarters behind it, year after year.[^iowa] TCU's Gary Patterson built a
[4-2-5](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4-2-5) (four linemen, two linebackers, five defensive
backs) around the same idea. When NFL defenses went looking for a two-high answer to the spread
offenses of the late 2010s, this is where the coaching knowledge was.

## Where quarters breaks

The holes of quarters follow directly from its rules. An offensive coordinator facing a quarters
team starts with three of them.

### Light-box runs

You've already seen the first, in the run-fit section: six in the box against six blockers, with
the safeties arriving late, and an offense that releases #2 or reads the safety with an RPO to take
one of them away. The other lever is simpler: **add a blocker.** Two-tight-end and fullback sets
make #2 a blocker who can block *the safety*, or put a seventh blocker against a six-man box so the
box is outnumbered before anyone arrives from depth; the heavier personnel of 2024 and 2025 was
partly this. The defense's counters are a front that holds its gaps without help (which is why
two-high defenses prize big interior linemen), safeties who tackle in space, and a willingness to
give up four-yard runs. [Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)
has the data on what runs against light boxes actually gain.

### The bootleg flood

Play-action attacks any coverage whose defenders read the run. Quarters is special because its
*deep* defenders read the run.

::: {#cell-fig-boot-flood .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def boot_play():
    off = [q.moved(w=8.5) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in offense("ace")]   # Z in a tight split
    dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
    mv = {"LCB": (7.5, -16.4), "RCB": (7.5, 9.3), "FS": (9.5, -6.0), "SS": (9.5, 5.5), "WILL": (4.5, -4.2)}
    dfn = [q.moved(d=mv[q.key][0], w=mv[q.key][1]) if q.key in mv else q for q in dfn]
    dfn = [q.moved(label="CB") if q.pos == "CB" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.6, 1.4)])
    p.block("Y", pts=[(0.5, 0.8)])
    p.path("RB", [(-4.5, 2.6), (-2.0, 5.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)                # the run fake
    p.path("QB", [(-3.2, 1.0), (-6.0, -2.5), (-6.5, -6.5)], absolute=True, speed=5.0)   # fake, then boot left
    p.route("X", r.go(24))
    p.route("U", [(0.6, 0.6), (0.7, 0.9), (1.8, 2.6), (3.5, 8.0)], speed=6.0)   # sells the block, then the flat
    p.route("Z", r.path((4, -1.5), (12, -13), (13.5, -21)))             # deep over, across the field
    p.pass_to("Z", t=2.9)
    p.drop("FS", (6.0, -5.0), speed=3.5)              # U's block says run: he steps up...
    p.drop("SS", (6.5, 4.8), speed=3.5)               # ...and so does the SS, keyed on Y
    p.drop("LCB", (21.0, -16.4), speed=5.5)           # MOD: X went deep, so he goes too
    p.drop("RCB", (11.0, 7.0), speed=4.6); p.drop("RCB", (13.6, -5.0), speed=4.6)   # trails Z across
    p.drop("WILL", (3.4, -3.8), speed=3.0); p.drop("WILL", (3.6, -9.6), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (3.0, 2.6), speed=3.0); p.drop("SAM", (3.0, 7.4), speed=3.0)
    p.highlight("FS", "Z")
    return p


boot = boot_play()
fld = clip(boot.draw(lateral=(-25, 14), window=(-9.5, 24.5), title=False))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, boot)
say(fld, boot, "FS: U's fake block says run,\nso he steps up; the over\nroute lands behind him", (18.4, 0.5), fs=6.3)
say(fld, boot, "CB: MOD, carries X", (22.6, -14.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, boot, "deep", (16.0, -18.4), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "~12 yd", (15.4, -12.4), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "flat", (4.8, -12.6), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "U: fakes a\nblock, then\nleaks out", (-4.0, -10.8), fs=6.0)
say(fld, boot, "trailing CB", (14.6, -2.2), fs=6.0)
plt.show()
```

The offense is in 12 personnel (two tight ends, U on the left and Y on the right; Z in a tight split), so the defense is in its base 4-3, with a Sam linebacker (S) next to the strong safety (SS). The offense fakes an outside zone run to the right and the quarterback rolls left. Three receivers flood the left side at three depths (the blue tags): X runs deep and the corner (MOD) carries him; U fakes a block for a beat, then leaks out to the flat; Z runs a deep over route from the far side and is caught at about 12 yards. The free safety (ringed) reads U, his #2, and U's fake block says run, so he steps up. The over route lands behind him and in front of the corner, with the corner from the other side trailing. Walk through it from the defense's side. The corner saw #1 go deep and went with him: correct,
MOD. The Will stepped up on the fake, then chased U to the flat: correct. The free safety read #2,
saw a block and came forward: correct by his rule, and wrong, because U's block was a fake. An
honest pass never fools a quarters safety; a pass dressed as a run can, because for a beat the fake
and the real thing look the same. The over route, coming from the other side of the field, entered the space between the
corner (deep with X) and the safety (up for the run) where *nobody's rule* put a defender: three
receivers at three depths on one side, against defenders whose first read sent them the wrong way.
The fake has to hold one more defender. On a bootleg the end on the side the quarterback rolls to
is usually left unblocked, so the quarterback is running toward a free rusher who must bite on the
run fake too.

It isn't that play-action is magic against quarters in particular. In the nflverse charting for
2023–2025, play-action raised the average result of a dropback against quarters by about as much
as it did against Cover 3 or Cover 1.[^pa] The point is *which* play-action. A run fake that pulls
the safeties forward, paired with a deep crosser from the far side, attacks the exact gap between
quarters' corner rule and its safety rule. The defense's counter is discipline in the read (safeties
taught to key through the blocker to the linemen and the quarterback, not just #2's first step) and
calls that tell the safety on the bootleg side to stay deep no matter what, at the cost of the run
fit.

### The running back's wheel

The third weakness hides in the rule for the apex defender: *take the first man to the flat.*

::: {#cell-fig-rb-wheel .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = [q.moved(w=2.3) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in spread_2x2()]   # back offset to the QB's right
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"NB": (4.8, 6.2), "WILL": (4.8, -2.4), "MIKE": (4.8, 1.6)}), los=35, to_go=None)
p.zone((19.0, 20.5), (8.0, 9.0), "empty")
p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 12)); p.route("Y", r.slant(2, 6))
p.route("RB", [(-3.8, 8.0), (-1.2, 12.6), (2.0, 17.6), (8.0, 20.2), (20.0, 20.8)], absolute=True, speed=7.5)
p.dropback(2.5); p.pass_to("RB", t=2.2)
protect(p)
p.drop("RCB", (10.6, 14.6), speed=5.0); p.drop("RCB", (11.8, 10.2), speed=5.0)   # MOD: #1 went deep, stay on him
p.drop("SS", (13.6, 7.6), speed=4.0)                                          # #2 not vertical: bracket #1
p.drop("MIKE", (5.6, 4.0), speed=4.0); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -2.0))
p.drop("NB", (5.4, 8.0), speed=3.0); p.drop("NB", (2.5, 12.5), speed=5.0)     # first man to the flat...
p.drop("NB", (4.0, 16.8), speed=5.0); p.drop("NB", (10.6, 19.0), speed=5.0)                                         # ...then chasing up the sideline
p.highlight("NB", "RB")
fld = clip(p.draw(lateral=(-5, 26.6), window=(-8.5, 25.0), title=False))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, "SS: #2 not vertical,\nso bracket #1's dig", (16.8, 7.0), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "CB: dig > 5 yd,\nMOD stays on #1", (6.6, 10.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "$: first man to the flat,\nnow chasing from behind", (-5.0, 18.4), fs=6.3)

Y (#2) runs a quick slant inside, so the strong safety, with no vertical #2, works inside and over the top to bracket Z's dig, and the Mike takes the slant. The running back (R, ringed, aligned to the quarterback's right) releases to the flat; the nickel ($, ringed) takes him as the first man to the flat, and then the back turns up the sideline.
